title: Quantized runtime routing and kernel guidance
body:
Purpose

Short working notes on constraints and runtime choices when serving quantized models (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ). This doc focuses on: kernel placement constraints, how quantization choices change scheduling and batching, and operational patterns for KV cache with quantized weights/activations. The goal: capture pragmatic constraints so runtime can (a) pick a fast path safely, (b) decide when to fallback to FP16/FP32, and (c) provide safe defaults for Dedicated/Private customers.

Status and audience
- Draft: meant for eng-serving-runtime, applied-ml, and release-engineering.
- Audience: runtime engineers implementing kernels and scheduler, perf engineers doing microbenchmarks, and solutions engineers validating enterprise deployments.

Scope and assumptions
- We assume upstream model conversion produces quantized checkpoints with metadata: per-tensor/per-channel scales, group-size, symmetric/asymmetric flags, and optional GPTQ/AWQ packing info.
- We assume hardware: NVIDIA GPUs (A100/H100), plus some AMDs. Primary fast paths target CUDA cuBLAS-like kernels and custom CUDA kernels.
- Latency SLO: 50–200ms p95 depending on model/route. Throughput targets vary per Dedicated pool.

High-level decisions (summary)
- Prefer integer compute kernels for matmul (INT8/FP8) only when: quantization metadata is compatible, activation distribution stable, and we can avoid expensive dequantize/requantize roundtrips.
- Fallback to FP16 path when: model uses per-token dynamic quantization (unsupported), group-size too small for vectorization, or KV cache interaction would cause large on-the-fly conversions that hurt latency.
- Support hybrid KV cache: keep KV in low-bit representation for long contexts when memory bound, but require a hot-path conversion cache (reconstructed FP16 for recent tokens) to avoid repeated conversions on critical latency path.

Kernel constraints (detailed)
1) Weight layout and memory alignment
   - INT8/FP8 kernels expect packed weight layouts: contiguous blocks of MxK aligned to 256 bytes to leverage tensor cores / warp-level MMA.
   - IF checkpoint has per-channel scales (out-channel quantization) kernel must support per-row scaling without extra scatter/gather. If not, fallback required.
   - AWQ/GPTQ packing often stores scale+packed groups; kernels must accept a pointer to "group metadata" and compute scaled dot-products without global dequantize.

2) GEMM semantics and fused ops
   - Fast path requires fused MatMul + Bias + Activation (e.g., Gelu/Swish) where possible to avoid memory traffic. For INT8, activation usually requires requantization to INT8 or going to FP16 mid-pipeline.
   - Attention kernels: fused QKV projection + reshape + attention compute (softmax) + output projection is ideal. Quantized attention must support correct scaling across softmax (softmax requires high-precision accumulator). Options:
     * Accumulate in FP32/FP16 internally, quantize outputs.
     * Use int32 accumulators with widened scaling (rare on GPUs).
   - Rotary/position embeddings: must be applied in the same precision as the matmul output. If rotary requires trig functions, prefer FP16 path unless precomputed rotations are quantized-compatible.

3) Activation and accumulator precision
   - For INT8 weights, accumulators must be at least int32 or FP16 to avoid overflow. Our CUDA kernels use FP16 accumulation by default when using tensor cores; ensure scale factors convert correctly.
   - FP8 inference requires careful calibration of exponent bias and dynamic range. Only enable FP8 path when conversion metadata includes exponent bias and per-layer clipping thresholds.

Scheduling implications
- Batch shape sensitivity: INT8/FP8 kernels often have better peak throughput but worse single-request latency when conversions are needed. Scheduler heuristics:
  - Small-batch/low-latency routes: prefer FP16 path or pre-warmed quantized paths with pinned memory.
  - High-throughput routes: prefer INT8/FP8 grouped GEMMs and larger batching windows.
  - Adaptive routing: use request size, recent token-per-second, and model-tag to decide routing. Maintain counters per-client for warm-start heuristics.

- Warm-up cost: first requests on a quantized model often trigger kernel JIT/initialization and possible on-the-fly dequantization. Scheduler should gate cold-starts behind small batch ramp to avoid p95 spikes.

KV cache interactions (memory vs CPU/GPU compute tradeoffs)
- Default: store KV cache in FP16 (easy, highest accuracy, simpler kernels).
- Memory-optimized option: store KV cache in INT8/AWQ format to reduce memory footprint (2–4x reduction). Tradeoffs:
  - Reading quantized KV requires per-access dequantize before attention compute or modifying attention kernel to accept quantized KV with appropriate accumulation scaling.
  - Frequent dequantize on hot tokens kills latency. Solution: maintain a small hot-cache of recently-used KV in FP16 alongside main quantized KV store.

- Heuristics for hot-cache population:
  - Keep last N tokens per stream in FP16 where N tuned by perf tests (default N=128 for long-context models).
  - When context length > threshold (e.g., 1024), evict cold tokens from FP16 hot-cache to quantized store.
  - Use LRU per-stream or per-request sequence position policy.

Hybrid calling pattern (recommended runtime flow)
1) On model load, parse quant metadata. If metadata incomplete, mark model as `quant-metadata-missing` and route to FP16 path.
2) During request scheduling: if route is latency-sensitive and model supports fast quant path, check hot-cache coverage. If full coverage, use quantized kernels.
3) If hot-cache miss: if miss count small, convert on-the-fly and populate hot-cache; if miss rate high, fallback to FP16 or throttle batching to amortize conversions.
4) Periodic background job: compress older KV regions to quantized store asynchronously.

Safety and quality considerations
- Bit-exactness not guaranteed across quant paths. For customer-facing stability guarantee, implement `pinned-model-version` + `preferred-precision` attributes so customers can pin to FP16/INT8 variants.
- Regression monitoring: add per-model prompt-set evals comparing FP16 vs quantized outputs. Alert when semantic divergence above threshold.

Testing and benchmarks
- Microbenchmarks to add:
  - Matmul peak for the quantized kernel across M,K,N dims used by our model zoo.
  - Attention end-to-end with quantized KV read: measure p50/p95 token latency and conversion overhead.
  - KV hot-cache hit/miss stress test: simulate long history and frequent random access.
  - Memory footprint surveys for typical customer context lengths (512/1024/2048/4096).
- Data to record in results: throughput (tokens/sec), token p95 latency, GPU memory usage, CPU conversion CPU%.

Rollout strategy
- Phase 0: internal experimental builds. Enable on dev clusters with opt-in flag: runtime.enable_quant_paths=true. Collect metrics to `quant-paths-dev` dashboards.
- Phase 1: limited beta on Dedicated hosts. Expose feature to customers with explicit `enable_quant` flag.
- Phase 2: general availability after two weeks of stable metrics and resolved open issues.

Open questions / unresolved items
- AWQ streaming: can AWQ group metadata be stored compactly and referenced per-layer without hurting coalesced memory reads? (Marcus to prototype memory layout).
- FP8 exponent management: best practice for per-layer clipping vs global dynamic range—needs experiments with H100 kernels.
- Autoscaler interaction: how to surface increased CPU usage from on-the-fly dequantize to autoscaler so we avoid noisy neighbors?
- Should we add an explicit "kv_storage_format" per-model route (choices: fp16|int8|hybrid) surfaced in API?

Action items
- Marcus: prototype int8 attention kernel accepting quantized KV and int32 accumulation (due 2025-03-10).
- Sofia: build microbench harness for KV hot-cache experiments (due 2025-03-07).
- Daniel: add metric set for quant-paths (flags, fallback rate, kv-quantization-ratio) and dashboard stub (due 2025-03-05).
- Aditi: draft API proposal for `kv_storage_format` and `preferred_precision` (due 2025-03-04).

Appendix: quick reference of behaviors by quant type
- INT8: best throughput, requires int32/FP16 accumulators, per-channel scales common, good when weights stable.
- FP8: high compression with hardware support on H100; fragile w.r.t. dynamic range, needs exponent metadata, good throughput but riskier for QA.
- GPTQ: group-wise scales, often offline-permuted weights; kernels must accept permuted packing and group-scales. Good tradeoff for very large dense models.
- AWQ: aggressive weight packing and quantization; minimal metadata but requires custom unpack on the fly. Great memory reduction but increases runtime complexity.

Notes to self: keep examples and microbench configs in repo at github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/quant-kernels (PR stub linked above). This doc should be iterative; expect followups after first prototypes land.
